title: Address
body:
Memory location

Every [[Byte]] of [[Memory]] has a number, and that number is its address. A [[Variable]] is a
name the compiler keeps for one; a [[Pointer]] is a variable whose *value* is one.

```c++
int i = 7;
int *p = &i;     // &i is the address of i
cout << *p;      // 7: the value at that address
```

`&` takes an address, `*` follows one. Those two operators are the whole of indirection, and
everything built on it ([[Dynamic Allocation]], [[Node]]s, [[Linked Structure]]s) is those two
symbols applied repeatedly.

An address is just an integer, which is why `p + 1` means something: it advances by one
element, not one byte, because the pointer's type says how big an element is. That is what
makes `a[i]` and `*(a + i)` the same expression; see [[Index]].

What addresses look like from underneath (the address bus, word alignment, why an odd address
can fault) is [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]]: [[System Bus]], [[Data representation]].

The *range* of addresses a program is allowed to name, and the fact that the numbers here are
virtual rather than physical, is [[Address Space]] in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]].
